case.display_title: Two weeks of bleeding gums and nosebleeds

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on bleeding from the gums and nose with visible haematuria. We reviewed the Chart so far. Bleeding from several mucosal sites at once points to a general haemostatic problem rather than a local one. If the platelet count is normal and the PT and APTT are both prolonged, this is a coagulation-factor problem: deficiency or antagonism of the vitamin K-dependent factors, liver disease, consumption or an inhibitor are the main possibilities, and normal fibrinogen and D-dimer would make consumption unlikely. If the clotting times are markedly prolonged, treat without waiting for the factor assays. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Give intravenous vitamin K now
Mixing study
Factor assays: II, V, VII, IX and X (with VIII if the APTT is out of proportion)
Fibrinogen, D-dimer and a blood film if not already done
Ask about anticoagulant medicines in the household and about rat poison
Group and save; hold off invasive procedures until the clotting improves

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to review the factor assays. Factors II, VII, IX and X are all very low while factor V is normal, with normal fibrinogen and D-dimer. That pattern is typical of vitamin K deficiency or a vitamin K antagonist, not of liver disease (factor V would also be low) or consumption. Diet alone rarely drives factors this low, and he takes no warfarin, so an undisclosed anticoagulant, including a long-acting one, must be excluded. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Continue intravenous vitamin K daily and follow the INR
Send an anticoagulant rodenticide panel and a warfarin level
Repeat the history of possible exposures, including food, travel and the household
Prothrombin complex concentrate only for life-threatening bleeding

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on management now that the anticoagulant rodenticide panel is positive. Long-acting agents of this kind persist in the body for months, which explains the partial and unstable response to 10 mg doses of vitamin K. The coagulopathy will recur if vitamin K is stopped early. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Oral vitamin K 100 mg daily on discharge, for months
INR at least weekly at first, then according to stability
Continue until the INR stays normal off treatment; consider repeating the level
Safety-net advice about bleeding; haematology clinic follow-up

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on an unexplained coagulopathy with bleeding. We reviewed the Chart so far. When the PT and APTT are both prolonged in a patient who says he takes no anticoagulant, an unrecognised exposure to a coumarin-type anticoagulant should be considered, whether from medicines in the household, rodenticides at home or work, contaminated products, or the food chain. Many exposed patients are unaware of it. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Warfarin level and an anticoagulant rodenticide panel
Detailed exposure history: household medicines, pest control, products used, foods
High-dose vitamin K; expect a slow response if a long-acting agent is involved

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise after a positive anticoagulant rodenticide panel. The patient reports no use of rodenticide at home or at work. Exposure can be indirect, through contaminated food or other products or through contact at work, so a careful exposure history covering unusual foods or products, including while abroad, is worth taking; intentional ingestion by the patient or by another person should also be considered sensitively. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Take a detailed exposure history: unusual foods or products, including while abroad, and contact at work
Consider a sensitive assessment for intentional exposure if no source is found
Oral vitamin K 50-100 mg daily, guided by the INR, for months
Report to the regional poisons centre

consult_notes.note_text: Asked about bleeding in a man with chronic hepatitis B on tenofovir. We reviewed the Chart. The endoscopy before admission showed no upper gastrointestinal source; the blood was coming from the mouth. Suppressed hepatitis B without signs of chronic liver disease would not usually prolong the clotting times this much; liver disease would lower factor V and fibrinogen as well. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Liver tests, albumin and factor V
Liver ultrasound and elastography as part of routine hepatitis B care
Continue tenofovir
No repeat endoscopy or liver biopsy while the clotting is uncorrected

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to review gum bleeding. We saw him before admission and prescribed tranexamic acid, without improvement. The gums ooze from the margins without a local dental cause to explain it, and he is also bleeding from the nose and into the urine. This points to a general bleeding problem rather than a dental one. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Investigate a systemic bleeding disorder
Soft toothbrush and chlorhexidine mouthwash; local pressure for oozing
Defer dental extractions and scaling until the clotting is corrected

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to review the nosebleeds. Anterior rhinoscopy shows dried blood and oozing at the left nostril without a single bleeding vessel. Recurrent nosebleeds together with gum and urinary bleeding suggest a general bleeding disorder. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Correct the clotting defect
Local pressure; nasal packing only if bleeding persists
Avoid cautery until the clotting improves

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to review visible haematuria in a man who is also bleeding from the gums and nose. We reviewed the Chart. Bleeding from several sites suggests the haematuria is part of a general bleeding problem. If renal function is normal and the urine shows red cells of uniform appearance without casts, a glomerular cause is unlikely. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Correct the coagulopathy and repeat the urinalysis
Renal tract ultrasound; urology review if haematuria persists once clotting is normal
No renal biopsy

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to assess whether the bleeding could be self-inflicted. We spoke with him. He is worried about the bleeding, his mood is reactive and appropriate, and he denies any thoughts of self-harm, now or in the past. There is no history of mental illness or substance misuse, and nothing suggests he is fabricating symptoms. We found no evidence of deliberate self-poisoning. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: No psychiatric follow-up needed on current evidence
Continue to look for an accidental source of exposure
Ask sensitively about the safety of the household

consult_notes.note_text: Asked about lupus, given his sister's diagnosis. He has no rash, mouth ulcers or joint symptoms. A family history alone does not explain mucosal bleeding of this kind; lupus usually bleeds through a low platelet count, so check that first. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: ANA and complement if not already done
Lupus anticoagulant testing is hard to interpret while the clotting factors are low

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on diabetes control. He admits often missing his metformin. After recent blood loss an HbA1c will underestimate his average glucose, so interpret it with capillary glucose readings. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Plasma glucose, HbA1c and capillary glucose monitoring during admission
Support adherence to metformin
Add a second agent if control remains poor
Diabetes clinic follow-up

consult_notes.note_text: Asked about infection after a month in China. He has been back two months and is afebrile. Without fever, and if the platelet count and renal function are normal, a viral haemorrhagic fever, dengue or leptospirosis is unlikely. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Dengue and leptospira serology only if fever develops
Continue tenofovir

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to review the diet. He eats mostly leftover meats and very few vegetables or fruit. That may lower his vitamin K intake, but diet alone rarely causes bleeding of this degree in an adult who is otherwise absorbing normally. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Increase green vegetables and fruit
Diabetes-appropriate dietary advice
Review again after discharge

must_do.text: Give vitamin K promptly (intravenously while bleeding) for bleeding with a markedly prolonged PT and APTT
Define the defect: vitamin K-dependent factor assays (II, VII, IX, X) with factor V as the control, or at least a mixing study
Ask about anticoagulant medicines and rat poison at home and at work
Send an anticoagulant rodenticide panel when no warfarin exposure explains a vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency
Take a detailed travel and dietary history, including unusual foods eaten abroad
Plan months of high-dose oral vitamin K with regular INR checks after discharge
Involve haematology in the work-up and long-term follow-up

must_not_do.text: Treat the bleeding with tranexamic acid alone, without vitamin K
Discharge without long-term high-dose vitamin K once the INR first improves (long-acting rodenticides persist for months)
Order a liver or kidney biopsy while the coagulopathy is uncorrected
Start anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs, including pharmacological thromboprophylaxis
Conclude deliberate self-poisoning without first taking a full dietary and travel history

ground_truth.outcome: INR labile between 1.00 and 1.91 over the next three months; 0.94 four months after discharge on oral vitamin K 100 mg daily. No further bleeding.
red_herrings: alcohol at a party several weeks earlier
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and dental referral

rubric.text: Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning, with eating animals bought at a street market abroad identified as the likely source
Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning, source not identified
Vitamin K deficiency coagulopathy without naming a long-acting anticoagulant
Coagulopathy of liver disease, DIC, acquired haemophilia, warfarin over-anticoagulation or deliberate self-poisoning as the final diagnosis
Unrelated diagnosis, or one that would lead to harm

teaching_points: A prolonged PT and APTT with normal platelets, fibrinogen and D-dimer, and low factors II, VII, IX and X with a normal factor V, is the signature of vitamin K deficiency or antagonism rather than liver disease or DIC.
When no warfarin is involved, a long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide is the leading cause; test for it and ask again about exposure, including food.
Long-acting rodenticides persist for months: standard vitamin K doses give an incomplete, unstable response, and treatment needs high-dose oral vitamin K for months with INR monitoring.
Rodenticides accumulate in the food chain: eating rodents, or animals that prey on them, is a possible route of exposure.
ground_truth.treatment_given: Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg: four doses over 48 hours, then 13 more doses during the admission; bleeding stopped, APTT normalised and the INR fell to 2.04 at discharge. Discharged on oral vitamin K 100 mg daily with haematology follow-up for INR monitoring.

reports.impression: Normocytic anaemia with mild polychromasia; platelets normal; no fragments.
reports.report_text: Red cells are normocytic and normochromic with mild anisocytosis and occasional polychromatic cells. No red cell fragments, spherocytes or inclusions. White cells are normal in number and morphology. Platelets are adequate in number with normal morphology.

reports.impression: Mild regenerative normocytic anaemia; no features of a microangiopathic process, marrow infiltration or a platelet disorder.
reports.report_text: Film reviewed by a haematopathologist. Normocytic normochromic red cells with mild anisocytosis and some polychromasia. No red cell fragments, spherocytes, target cells or inclusions. Leucocytes show normal maturation and morphology, with no blasts or atypical cells. Platelets are adequate in number and morphologically unremarkable. Comment: the film does not explain the prolonged clotting times; correlate with coagulation factor assays.

reports.impression: No upper gastrointestinal bleeding source; bleeding from the mouth.
reports.report_text: Outpatient endoscopy before this admission, to the second part of the duodenum. Normal oesophageal, gastric and duodenal mucosa. No ulcer, varices or source of bleeding in the oesophagus or stomach. Fresh blood was seen in the oral cavity.
Complete colonoscopy to the caecum with intubation of the terminal ileum; adequate bowel preparation. Normal mucosa throughout; no polyps, ulceration, angiodysplasia or source of bleeding.

reports.impression: Mild fatty infiltration of the liver; no features of cirrhosis or portal hypertension; debris in the bladder.
reports.report_text: The liver is normal in size (15 cm) with a smooth outline and mildly increased echogenicity; no focal lesion. The portal vein is of normal calibre with hepatopetal flow. The spleen is normal in size (10.5 cm). No ascites. The gallbladder, bile ducts, pancreas and both kidneys appear normal. The bladder is partly filled and contains a little echogenic debris.

reports.impression: Liver stiffness within the range expected without significant fibrosis; mild steatosis.
reports.report_text: Ten valid measurements obtained. Median liver stiffness 6.2 kPa with an interquartile range under 30% of the median. Controlled attenuation parameter 268 dB/m.

reports.impression: Mild chronic hepatitis with minimal activity and no significant fibrosis; mild steatosis.
reports.report_text: Core of liver with eleven portal tracts. Mild portal lymphocytic inflammation with minimal interface activity; occasional ground-glass hepatocytes. Mild macrovesicular steatosis (about 10% of hepatocytes). No bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis on reticulin and Masson trichrome. Perls stain shows no excess iron.

reports.impression: Normal kidneys; mobile debris in the bladder in keeping with blood.
reports.report_text: Both kidneys are normal in size (right 10.8 cm, left 11.1 cm) with preserved corticomedullary differentiation. No calculi, mass or pelvicalyceal dilatation. The bladder contains a little mobile echogenic debris; the bladder wall is smooth and no mass is seen.

reports.impression: No calculus or obstruction; blood in the bladder.
reports.report_text: Non-contrast CT of the urinary tract. No urinary tract calculi. No hydronephrosis, hydroureter or perinephric stranding. Slightly dense fluid layering in the bladder, in keeping with blood; no bladder wall thickening.
Non-contrast CT of the head. No intracranial haemorrhage, mass effect or midline shift. Grey-white matter differentiation is preserved. The ventricles and extra-axial spaces are normal for age.

vignette: A 37-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and chronic hepatitis B on tenofovir presents with two weeks of intermittent bleeding from the gums and nose and two days of blood in his urine.
